description: A European edible crab known for its sweet meat and compact body; commonly associated with rocky and sandy marine seabeds.
context: WWF rates French Crab Reduce. Its stock is described as data-limited, although available landing information and adjacent-area evidence indicate abundance and fishing rate are stable enough for long-term productivity. WWF also notes that pot fisheries generally have minor ecosystem effects and are unlikely to cause significant damage to endangered species. Those mixed conditions support Reduce rather than Best Choice.

description: A soft-shell mud crab harvested shortly after moulting, with a tender shell and meat that can be eaten whole.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Ketam Lembut produced in trays as Avoid. Soft-shell crab refers to mud crabs harvested shortly after moulting, while their new shell is still soft. WWF notes that the crabs used for this production are taken from the wild and subsequently cultured in trays. Dependence on wild-caught crabs can place additional pressure on natural mud crab populations, particularly where stocks are affected by overfishing and loss of mangrove habitat.

description: A mangrove-associated mud crab valued across Southeast Asia, typically found in estuaries, mudflats and coastal wetlands.
context: WWF rates Malaysian wild-caught Ketam Bakau caught using traps as Avoid. Mud crabs are mainly found in estuarine and sheltered coastal habitats, with large populations commonly associated with established mangroves. WWF reports that mud crab populations are declining mainly due to overfishing and destruction of mangrove habitat. Although traps are relatively targeted, declining populations and loss of important coastal habitat remain major sustainability concerns.

description: A fast-growing swimming crab found in coastal waters, widely traded for its delicate, sweet meat.
context: WWF rates Ketam Bunga / Ketam Biru from Sabah caught using traps as Reduce. This species can be relatively resilient to fishing pressure, but stocks in the wider region are not always well monitored and some populations have experienced high fishing pressure. Trap fisheries are generally selective with relatively low bycatch and limited seabed impacts, but maintaining healthy breeding populations and controlling fishing pressure remain important for sustainability.

description: A large cold-water king crab prized for its substantial legs and sweet meat, associated with northern Pacific waters.
context: WWF rates Raja Ketam from Alaska caught using pots or traps as Best Choice. Alaska’s red king crab fisheries are managed through stock assessments, catch limits, minimum size requirements and regulated fishing seasons to help maintain sustainable populations. Pots and traps are relatively selective fishing methods that allow undersized and many non-target animals to be released, while generally causing less seabed disturbance than mobile bottom fishing gears. These management measures and the relatively selective fishing method support its Best Choice rating.

description: A cold-water schooling whitefish that forms an important commercial fishery in the North Pacific.
context: WWF notes that Alaska pollock shares waters with endangered, threatened and protected species including Steller sea lions, Chinook salmon and sharks. Bycatch is relatively low and discards have decreased, but the species is ecologically important and continued fishing may alter food-web structure. Bottom-trawl habitat impacts are assessed as moderate because fishing occurs partly over sponge beds and sedimentary habitats.

description: A highly migratory tuna with firm, pale meat, commonly found in temperate and tropical open-ocean waters.
context: WWF notes that Albacore Tuna is highly migratory and listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. A previous southern-stock assessment led to a lower total allowable catch after the stock was considered overfished; the updated assessment cited by WWF no longer considered that stock overfished or undergoing overfishing. The South African pole-and-line record is consequently rated Best Choice in this guide.

description: A large, fast-swimming tuna that migrates across the open Atlantic and is highly valued in premium seafood markets.
context: WWF highlights very high bycatch in Atlantic pelagic longline fisheries, including protected seabirds such as albatrosses and petrels, as well as vulnerable sharks, marine mammals, sea turtles and billfishes. Bluefin also occupies a high trophic level, so heavy fishing can affect wider food webs. Although pelagic longlines do not damage sensitive benthic habitats, WWF still rates this record Avoid.

description: A cold-water cod species associated with northern Atlantic waters and valued for its mild, flaky flesh.
context: WWF reports that the North-East Arctic cod stock was healthy in its cited assessment and covered by a good management plan. Spatial and temporal closures protect juveniles and help control fishing, while management measures also help reduce illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. Despite these positive factors, this Russian Barents Sea record is classified Reduce under WWF's assessment.

description: A widely farmed salmon with pink-orange flesh, raised in marine cages and commonly sold fresh or smoked.
context: WWF explains that Norwegian floating net-pen salmon farms directly interact with the marine environment. Fish waste, uneaten feed and antibiotics can enter surrounding waters and sediments, while escapes, disease, parasites and chemical use can affect ecosystems. These environmental risks are why the floating-cage farmed salmon record is placed in WWF's Reduce category.

description: A small tropical tuna that travels in schools through warm ocean waters and is widely used in Southeast Asian fisheries.
context: WWF rates Bakulan from Sabah caught using purse seine as Reduce. Skipjack tuna is a fast-growing and highly productive tuna species that generally withstands fishing pressure better than larger tuna species. Purse seine fishing can efficiently target large schools, but sustainability depends on controlling fishing pressure and reducing the capture of juvenile tuna and other non-target species. Responsible management of the fishery is therefore important to maintain healthy stocks.

description: A sea cucumber species living on shallow sandy and muddy seabeds, harvested for its dried sea-cucumber product.
context: WWF rates Bangkuli / Balat from Sabah farmed in sea pens as Avoid. Sandfish is a sea cucumber that plays an important ecological role by processing organic material in seabed sediments. Wild populations have experienced heavy harvesting pressure because of their high commercial value, and depleted populations can recover slowly when breeding adults become scarce. Although sea-pen farming can support production, responsible sourcing of juveniles and management of farming activities are important to avoid adding pressure to vulnerable wild populations.

description: A warm-water pompano with a streamlined body, often associated with coastal waters and marine aquaculture.
context: WWF rates Bawal Emas Best Choice for Malaysian Peninsular cage culture. The guide describes snubnose pompano as an Indo-Pacific species associated with rocky reefs, coral reefs and inshore habitats and notes that it is a popular aquaculture species in Malaysia. WWF's Best Choice category is reserved for preferred seafood from well-managed stocks or lower-impact aquaculture.

description: A deep-bodied pomfret with a distinctive dark body, commonly sold in Malaysian seafood markets.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Bawal Hitam caught using trawl as Reduce. Bawal Hitam is a commercially important coastal fish found over continental shelf waters. Trawl fishing can catch a wide range of non-target fish and marine organisms alongside the target species and may disturb seabed habitats when the gear contacts the bottom. Managing fishing pressure and reducing unwanted catch are therefore important for improving the sustainability of this fishery.

description: A silver-bodied pomfret found over muddy coastal seabeds and widely consumed across Asian markets.
context: WWF notes that Chinese Silver Pomfret occurs seasonally, usually singly or in small schools over muddy bottoms, and may enter estuaries. The guide states that it is mainly caught by trawl and describes trawling as highly detrimental because it is non-selective, prone to habitat destruction and can create bycatch of endangered, threatened and protected species. These impacts support Avoid.

description: A coastal mullet associated with estuaries and shallow waters, recognised for its elongated body and fine-textured flesh.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Belanak caught using gillnets as Best Choice. Belanak is a coastal fish commonly associated with shallow waters and estuaries and can tolerate a wide range of environmental conditions. Gillnets can efficiently target fish of particular sizes when appropriate mesh sizes are used, although poorly managed nets may also catch non-target marine animals. Under the fishery assessed by WWF, this source is considered a preferred seafood choice.

description: A small anchovy-like fish used locally as dried or salted seafood and associated with Malaysian coastal fisheries.
context: WWF rates Bulu Ayam (Ikan Masin) from Peninsular Malaysia caught using seine nets as Reduce. This small coastal fish is commonly harvested for drying and salting and forms part of Malaysia's small-fish fisheries. Seine fishing can capture large numbers of fish at once and may also retain juvenile and non-target species depending on the fishing area and mesh size used. Maintaining appropriate fishing pressure and reducing unwanted catch are important for the long-term sustainability of the fishery.

description: A small silver fish that lives over sandy and muddy coastal bottoms and is commonly caught in nearshore fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Bulus caught using trawl as Avoid. Bulus is a bottom-associated coastal fish commonly found over sandy and muddy seabeds. Its habitat overlaps with areas where trawling operates, and trawl fishing can disturb seabed communities while capturing juvenile and non-target marine species together with the target catch. These impacts make responsible management of fishing effort and seabed habitats particularly important.

description: A robust coastal scad that forms schools in tropical waters and is a familiar fish in Malaysian markets.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Cencaru caught using purse seine, gillnets and trawl as Best Choice. Cencaru is a schooling coastal fish that is widely harvested in Malaysian waters. Purse seines can efficiently target schools in the water column, while gillnets and trawls have different levels of bycatch and habitat impact. Sustainability therefore depends on appropriate management of fishing effort, gear use and the condition of the stock. Under the fisheries assessed by WWF, this source is considered a preferred seafood choice.

description: A large Pacific salmon known for its rich flavour and dark flesh, migrating between the ocean and freshwater rivers.
context: WWF says Alaskan Chinook salmon fisheries are managed by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and that the cited stocks are healthy. The guide notes commercial regulations for individual fishing areas, participation in Fishery Improvement Projects and partial MSC certification. These stock and management measures support the Best Choice classification for the Alaskan fishery.

description: A sea cucumber found on shallow reef and coastal seabeds, harvested as a marine invertebrate seafood product.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Gamat / Timun Laut collected by hand as Avoid. Sea cucumbers play an important ecological role on the seabed by consuming organic material and recycling nutrients within marine sediments. Hand collection causes relatively little physical habitat damage, but sea cucumbers are vulnerable to overharvesting because high-value populations can be rapidly depleted when too many adults are removed. Maintaining sufficient breeding populations is therefore particularly important for their recovery and long-term sustainability.

description: A long-bodied cold-water fish commonly caught around New Zealand and used widely as a white-fleshed seafood.
context: WWF notes that New Zealand hoki is caught with mid-water otter trawls. Bycatch is estimated at about 12% of catch and juveniles at 20–30%, while interactions with endangered, threatened and protected species may be high. Discard rates are low and seabed contact is considered unlikely, limiting habitat impact. The combination of risks and mitigations leads WWF to Reduce.

description: Small schooling anchovies widely used fresh, dried or fermented in Malaysian cuisine and coastal food traditions.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Ikan Bilis caught using purse seines and lift nets as Reduce. Ikan Bilis are small schooling fish that form an important part of marine food webs by transferring energy from plankton to larger fish, seabirds and other predators. Purse seines and lift nets can harvest large quantities from dense schools, so excessive fishing can affect both the target population and species that depend on these fish as prey. Sustainable harvesting therefore requires appropriate control of fishing pressure.

description: A colourful fusilier that forms schools around reefs and coastal waters, often encountered in tropical Southeast Asian fisheries.
context: WWF describes this fishery as data deficient, with no stock characterisation or indirect stock-status indicators in Malaysia and limited information on the species' biology. Given widespread overfishing across the Indo-Pacific, WWF considers stocks likely to be overfished or undergoing overfishing. The guide also says bottom-set gillnets are non-selective and can have high impacts on endangered, threatened and protected species. This supports Avoid.

description: A group of coastal croakers that often live near muddy bottoms and estuaries and produce characteristic drumming sounds.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Ikan Gelama caught using bottom trawl as Avoid. Ikan Gelama are bottom-associated coastal fish commonly found over sandy and muddy substrates and in estuarine environments. Bottom trawling can disturb these seabed habitats and capture a broad range of non-target fish and invertebrates alongside the target catch. The combination of fishing pressure, bycatch and seabed disturbance creates significant sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A red snapper associated with reefs and coastal waters, known for firm flesh and a bright reddish body.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Ikan Merah caught using hook and line as Reduce. Ikan Merah is a reef-associated snapper that can be vulnerable to sustained fishing pressure because larger individuals take time to reach maturity and contribute significantly to reproduction. Hook-and-line fishing is relatively selective and generally causes little direct damage to seabed habitats, although maintaining healthy breeding populations and appropriate fishing pressure remains important for the long-term sustainability of the stock.

description: A bottom-dwelling flatfish with both eyes on one side of its body, living mainly over sandy or muddy seabeds.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Ikan Sebelah caught using bottom trawl as Avoid. Ikan Sebelah are bottom-dwelling flatfish that live on sandy and muddy seabeds, placing them directly within habitats affected by bottom trawling. Bottom trawls can disturb seabed communities and capture juvenile fish and other non-target marine species alongside the target catch. The combination of fishing pressure, bycatch and disturbance to the benthic habitat creates significant sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A small schooling scad common in tropical waters and a familiar fish in Malaysian seafood markets.
context: WWF notes that Common Scad is a schooling species found mainly in open water and commonly around insular habitats, with catches often coming from roughly 40–200 metres. The guide says stock health and species biology information is lacking, creating uncertainty about sustainability. Purse seine is described as the common and more selective harvest method, so WWF assigns Reduce rather than Avoid.

description: A snapper associated with coastal and reef habitats, recognised for its coppery-red body and firm flesh.
context: WWF reports that no stock assessments are available for John's Snapper and that the species is highly vulnerable to fishing pressure. Regional fisheries are considered significantly overfished, while bottom trawling can threaten turtles and damage corals and other benthic organisms. The guide also notes high catches of juveniles and non-target fish and insufficient information to judge management effectiveness. These factors support Avoid.

description: A broad group of sharks that occupy many marine habitats and play important roles as ocean predators.
context: WWF highlights overfishing and demand for shark fins and meat as major pressures on sharks. The guide also emphasises that sharks are important predators within marine ecosystems and that WWF is working to reduce unsustainable fishing and demand. Given these conservation pressures and the Malaysia/global wild-caught context, the entire shark category is placed in Avoid.

description: A fast predatory barracuda found in tropical coastal waters, recognisable by its elongated body and strong jaws.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kekacang caught using trawl as Avoid. Kekacang is a predatory barracuda found in tropical coastal and offshore waters. Trawl fishing can capture non-target fish and other marine organisms alongside the target catch and may disturb seabed habitats where the gear contacts the bottom. These impacts, together with the need to manage fishing pressure on predatory fish populations, create sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A small schooling mackerel widely eaten in Malaysia, with oily flesh and a strong place in everyday local cuisine.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kembung / Pelaling caught using purse seine as Reduce. This schooling mackerel is an important small pelagic fish in Malaysian fisheries and also forms part of the marine food web as prey for larger predators. Purse seines can efficiently harvest large schools, making appropriate control of fishing effort important to prevent excessive pressure on the stock. Maintaining healthy populations is important both for the fishery and for the wider marine ecosystem.

description: A small grouper associated with reef and rocky coastal habitats and valued for its firm, white flesh.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Bebeh from Peninsular Malaysia caught using trawl as Avoid. Kerapu Bebeh is a reef-associated grouper, and groupers can be vulnerable to sustained fishing pressure because many species grow relatively slowly and depend on mature adults for successful reproduction. Trawling can also capture non-target species and disturb seabed habitats, adding further environmental impacts to the fishery.

description: A reef-associated grouper found in tropical coastal waters, commonly sold as a premium food fish in Southeast Asia.
context: WWF notes that Orange Spotted Grouper uses coastal habitats including mangroves, coral reefs, estuaries, shallow seas and saline lagoons. It is commonly caught by bottom trawl, which the guide describes as highly detrimental because the gear is non-selective, can damage habitat and can produce bycatch of endangered, threatened and protected species. The combined habitat and fishing-method risks support Avoid.

description: A grouper associated with tropical coastal habitats, with a sturdy body and firm, white flesh.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Ekor Gelap from Peninsular Malaysia caught using trawl as Avoid. Kerapu Ekor Gelap is a grouper associated with tropical coastal and reef habitats. Like many groupers, its populations can be vulnerable to sustained fishing pressure, particularly when mature individuals are heavily harvested. Trawl fishing adds further concern because it can capture non-target marine life and disturb seabed habitats.

description: A large, reef-associated grouper with a marbled pattern, commonly produced through marine cage aquaculture.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Harimau from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using cage culture as Reduce. Kerapu Harimau is a reef-associated grouper widely cultured as a high-value food fish. Cage farming can reduce direct fishing pressure on adult wild groupers when hatchery-produced juveniles are used, but sustainability depends on responsible sourcing of juveniles and feed and effective management of waste, disease and escapes.

description: A very large grouper that can inhabit reefs and coastal waters, reaching exceptional size compared with many groupers.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Kertang from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using cage culture as Avoid. Kerapu Kertang is a very large grouper that grows relatively slowly and is vulnerable to exploitation in the wild. Farming can reduce direct harvesting of adults, but sustainability depends on whether juveniles are hatchery-produced, how feed is sourced and how farms manage waste, disease and escapes. Reliance on marine resources for seed or feed can reduce the environmental benefits of aquaculture.

description: A large tropical grouper associated with coastal and reef habitats and known for its firm, white flesh.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Lumpur from Peninsular Malaysia caught using trawl as Avoid. Kerapu Lumpur is a large grouper associated with coastal, estuarine and reef habitats. Groupers can be vulnerable to fishing pressure because of their relatively slow growth and the importance of mature breeding individuals. Trawl fishing creates additional environmental concerns through non-target catch and disturbance of seabed habitats.

description: A brightly coloured reef grouper associated with coral habitats and highly valued in Southeast Asian seafood markets.
context: WWF describes this grouper fishery as data deficient, with no Malaysian stock assessments and indirect indicators showing major declines in fish productivity. The species is vulnerable to fishing pressure and linked to the high-value live reef fish trade. Although single handline is selective and has low habitat impact and bycatch, removal of reef top predators can affect trophic systems, and management is uneven. WWF therefore rates Avoid.

description: A distinctive grouper with a rounded profile, associated with reef habitats and increasingly encountered in aquaculture.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Tikus from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using cage culture as Avoid. Kerapu Tikus is a high-value reef-associated grouper that is vulnerable to exploitation and is commonly traded in the live reef fish market. Cage farming can reduce direct capture of adults when hatchery-produced juveniles are used, but sustainability depends on responsible juvenile and feed sourcing and effective management of waste, disease and escapes.

description: A humpback grouper recognised by its distinctive head and body shape, associated with tropical reef environments.
context: WWF rates Kerapu Tikus from Sabah caught using cyanide as Avoid. Cyanide fishing involves using poison to stun live reef fish for capture and can damage or kill corals and other reef organisms exposed to the chemical. It can also cause stress and mortality in captured fish. Because coral reefs provide essential habitat for Kerapu Tikus and many other marine species, this destructive fishing method can harm both the target population and the wider reef ecosystem.

description: A large trevally with a powerful build, commonly found around coastal reefs and deeper tropical waters.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kerepoh caught using trawl as Avoid. Kerepoh is a predatory fish associated with coastal and reef environments. Trawl fishing can capture juvenile and non-target marine species alongside the target catch and can disturb seabed habitats when the gear contacts the bottom. These environmental impacts, together with fishing pressure on larger predatory fish, create sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A small to medium coastal bream found over sandy or muddy bottoms and widely represented in Asian fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kerisi caught using trawl as Reduce. Kerisi are bottom-associated fish commonly found over sandy and muddy substrates in coastal and offshore waters. Trawling operates directly within these habitats and can capture non-target species while disturbing seabed communities. Managing fishing effort, bycatch and habitat impacts is therefore important for improving the sustainability of this fishery.

description: Small schooling ponyfish associated with coastal waters and sandy or muddy seabeds.
context: WWF rates Kikek from Sabah caught using lift nets as Reduce. Kikek is a small coastal fish commonly found in shallow marine waters and estuaries. Lift nets can target schooling fish with relatively little contact with the seabed, but they may capture juvenile and non-target fish depending on mesh size and fishing location. Managing fishing pressure and unwanted catch is therefore important for maintaining the sustainability of this fishery.

description: A small red snapper associated with tropical coastal habitats and commonly caught by bottom-oriented fishing gears.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kunyit-kunyit caught using trawl as Avoid. Kunyit-kunyit is a reef-associated snapper found in coastal waters and around coral and rocky habitats. Trawling can capture juvenile and non-target marine species and may disturb seabed habitats where the gear contacts the bottom. These impacts, together with fishing pressure on reef-associated fish populations, create sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A long-bodied threadfin that lives in coastal and estuarine waters and is valued for its firm flesh.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kurau caught using drift nets and gillnets as Reduce. Kurau is a commercially valuable coastal fish commonly associated with shallow waters, estuaries and muddy habitats. Gillnets can effectively target particular sizes of fish, but they can also accidentally entangle non-target marine animals. Maintaining healthy breeding populations and reducing unwanted catch are important for improving the sustainability of this fishery.

description: A large, slow-growing wrasse closely associated with coral reefs and recognisable by its thick lips and hump-shaped head.
context: WWF identifies Humphead Wrasse as a long-lived, slow-breeding coral-reef species and notes that it can reach very large sizes. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in CITES Appendix II. WWF identifies overfishing, habitat destruction, cyanide fishing and fish bombing as threats. These biological and conservation pressures make the Malaysian Sabah wild-caught record Avoid.

description: A schooling scad found in coastal and offshore waters and commonly landed in tropical Southeast Asian fisheries.
context: WWF rates Mata Besar / Lolong from Peninsular Malaysia caught using purse seine as Reduce. This schooling coastal fish forms large aggregations that can be efficiently targeted by purse seines. Although purse seine fishing generally has limited direct contact with seabed habitats, large catches can place pressure on stocks if fishing effort is not effectively controlled. Maintaining appropriate harvest levels is therefore important for sustaining the population.

description: A long, slender marine predator with a streamlined body, often found in tropical coastal and open-water habitats.
context: WWF rates Parang from Peninsular Malaysia caught using trawl as Avoid. Parang is a predatory coastal fish found in marine and estuarine waters. Trawl fishing can capture non-target fish and other marine organisms alongside the target catch and may disturb seabed habitats. These impacts, combined with fishing pressure on the target population, create sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A broad group of rays with flattened bodies and wing-like fins, found across many marine habitats.
context: WWF states that overfishing is the largest threat to rays. Some ray fins enter the shark-fin trade, while ray and skate meat is also consumed in coastal communities. Because the category covers multiple ray groups and the assessed fisheries use trawls and gillnets, WWF places the record in Avoid to reduce pressure on vulnerable ray populations and associated marine ecosystems.

description: A freshwater catfish farmed widely in Southeast Asia, valued for its mild flavour and soft, white flesh.
context: WWF rates Vietnamese farmed Pangasius Best Choice and records Aquaculture Stewardship Council certification. The guide's Best Choice category is for preferred seafood from well-managed stocks or aquaculture considered lower impact, while ASC certification provides an additional signal of responsible farming and traceability. For this record, the combination of farmed production and ASC certification supports the preferred-choice rating.

description: A small tropical scad that forms schools in coastal waters and is commonly caught by purse seine fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Pelata caught using purse seine as Reduce. Pelata is a small schooling fish found in coastal and offshore waters and forms part of the food supply for larger marine predators. Purse seines can efficiently harvest large schools with relatively little direct seabed impact, but excessive fishing can reduce the abundance of the target population. Appropriate control of fishing effort is therefore important for maintaining healthy stocks.

description: A small yellow-tailed scad associated with tropical coastal waters and commonly caught in nearshore fisheries.
context: WWF calls this a very data-deficient fishery: the species' biology and vulnerability to fishing mortality cannot be properly assessed. Given widespread overfishing in the Indo-Pacific and specifically Malaysia and Indonesia, the guide considers stocks likely to be overfished or undergoing overfishing. It also says bottom-set gillnets are non-selective and can have high impacts on endangered, threatened and protected species, supporting Avoid.

description: A mangrove-associated snapper that can live in estuaries and coastal waters and is valued as a food fish.
context: WWF rates Siakap Merah from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using cage and pond culture as Avoid. Siakap Merah is a mangrove-associated snapper that uses estuaries and coastal habitats during its life cycle. Cage and pond aquaculture can create sustainability concerns through feed sourcing, waste discharge, disease management and interactions with surrounding coastal environments. Responsible farm management is therefore important for reducing these impacts, and WWF identifies its Aquaculture Improvement Project as an alternative for this seafood source.

description: A versatile Asian seabass found in estuaries, coastal waters and farms, known for its mild flavour and firm flesh.
context: WWF highlights risks in Malaysian barramundi pond farming including effects on soil fertility and salinisation of soil and water bodies. The guide also notes that some small Malaysian farms depend on trash fish, resulting in a high Fish Feed Dependency Ratio. Although pond systems can have lower disease risk than open cages, WWF still rates this record Avoid and points consumers to AIP alternatives.

description: A small schooling sardine associated with warm coastal waters and widely used as a food fish in Southeast Asia.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Tamban / Sardin caught using purse seine as Reduce. Tamban / Sardin are small schooling pelagic fish that play an important role in marine food webs as prey for larger fish and other predators. Purse seines can efficiently harvest large schools and generally have limited direct seabed impact, but high fishing pressure can reduce populations and affect species that depend on them as food. Sustainable harvesting therefore requires appropriate management of fishing effort.

description: A large, fast-swimming mackerel with firm flesh, widely consumed in Malaysia and other tropical Asian markets.
context: WWF assesses the same Narrow-barred Spanish Mackerel species differently by fishing method. Hook-and-line is highly selective and has much lower bycatch and discard levels, so that record is Reduce; the gillnet record is Avoid. WWF also notes that the species is Near Threatened, stocks are not fully assessed across its range and catch data are limited. The method therefore materially affects the classification.

description: A large, fast-swimming mackerel with firm flesh, widely consumed in Malaysia and other tropical Asian markets.
context: WWF assesses the same Narrow-barred Spanish Mackerel species differently by fishing method. Hook-and-line is highly selective and has much lower bycatch and discard levels, so that record is Reduce; the gillnet record is Avoid. WWF also notes that the species is Near Threatened, stocks are not fully assessed across its range and catch data are limited. The method therefore materially affects the classification.

description: A long-bodied shad associated with coastal waters and river-influenced habitats, important in regional fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Terubok caught using gillnets as Reduce. Terubok is a coastal fish that migrates into estuarine and river environments for reproduction, making breeding populations particularly important to the sustainability of the fishery. Gillnets can effectively target fish but may also capture non-target species. Fishing pressure during migration and spawning periods can further affect the ability of the population to reproduce and recover.

description: A hardy freshwater tilapia commonly farmed for its mild flavour, firm flesh and adaptable production conditions.
context: WWF provides two Malaysian tilapia assessments. The general Malaysian cage/pond-culture record is Reduce, while the Hulu Perak cage-culture record is Best Choice and ASC certified. The guide notes that ASC-certified tilapia is available from Tasik Temenggor, Perak. This illustrates that production location and responsible farming practices can materially change the sustainability assessment.

description: A farmed Nile tilapia associated with freshwater culture systems and valued as an accessible, mild-flavoured food fish.
context: WWF provides two Malaysian tilapia assessments. The general Malaysian cage/pond-culture record is Reduce, while the Hulu Perak cage-culture record is Best Choice and ASC certified. The guide notes that ASC-certified tilapia is available from Tasik Temenggor, Perak. This illustrates that production location and responsible farming practices can materially change the sustainability assessment.

description: A tropical tuna that lives in coastal and offshore waters and is widely used in Southeast Asian fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Tongkol caught using purse seine as Reduce. Tongkol is a fast-swimming pelagic tuna that forms schools in tropical and subtropical waters. Purse seines can efficiently capture these schools with little direct impact on seabed habitats, but sustainability depends on maintaining appropriate fishing pressure and limiting the capture of juvenile and non-target species.

description: A small tropical tuna with firm flesh, commonly found in warm coastal and offshore waters.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Tongkol Kurik caught using purse seine as Reduce. Tongkol Kurik is a small tuna species that grows relatively quickly and forms schools in coastal and offshore waters. Purse seine fishing can efficiently target these aggregations, but large catches and the capture of juvenile or non-target fish can create sustainability concerns when fishing pressure is high. Effective management of fishing effort is therefore important for maintaining healthy stocks.

description: A small tuna species found in warm ocean waters, recognised by its compact body and strong swimming ability.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Tongkol Selasih caught using purse seine as Reduce. Tongkol Selasih is a small, fast-growing tuna found in tropical coastal and offshore waters. Its relatively rapid growth can make it more resilient than larger tuna species, but purse seine fisheries can remove large numbers of fish from schooling populations. Controlling fishing pressure and reducing juvenile and non-target catch are therefore important for the long-term sustainability of the fishery.

description: Tiny shrimp harvested for use fresh, dried or fermented, including as an ingredient in Malaysian belacan.
context: WWF rates Geragau / Belacan from Peninsular Malaysia caught using bag nets as Reduce. Geragau are tiny coastal shrimps commonly harvested for use fresh, dried or fermented, including in the production of belacan. Bag nets can retain very small marine organisms and may capture juvenile fish and other non-target species together with the shrimp. Managing fishing effort and reducing unwanted catch are therefore important for maintaining the sustainability of this coastal fishery.

description: A large tropical prawn widely farmed in ponds and valued for its firm flesh and distinctive striped appearance.
context: WWF rates Udang Harimau from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using pond culture as Reduce. Udang Harimau is a large tropical prawn commonly raised in coastal aquaculture ponds. Pond farming can create environmental pressures through water discharge, waste accumulation, feed use, disease and changes to surrounding coastal habitats when farms are not properly managed. Responsible management of water quality, feed, disease and farm effluent is therefore important for reducing these impacts. WWF also identifies its Aquaculture Improvement Project as an alternative for improving the sustainability of this seafood source.

description: A large marine crustacean with elongated limbs, living on or near the seabed and often sold whole.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Udang Lipan caught using trawl as Avoid. Udang Lipan are bottom-dwelling marine crustaceans that commonly live in burrows on sandy or muddy seabeds. Trawl fishing operates directly across these bottom habitats and can capture non-target fish and other marine organisms while disturbing seabed communities. The combination of bycatch and habitat disturbance creates significant sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A tropical banana prawn found in coastal waters and estuaries, commonly harvested in Southeast Asian fisheries.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Udang Putih caught using gillnets as Reduce. Udang Putih are coastal prawns commonly found in shallow waters and estuaries, with these habitats providing important nursery areas during their life cycle. Gillnets can catch the target species but may also entangle non-target fish and other marine animals depending on mesh size and fishing location. Managing fishing pressure and reducing unwanted catch are therefore important for maintaining the sustainability of this fishery.

description: A widely farmed tropical prawn with a pale body, valued for its mild flavour and dependable aquaculture performance.
context: WWF rates Udang Putih Pasifik from Peninsular Malaysia farmed using pond culture as Reduce. Pond farming of prawns can create environmental pressures through water discharge, waste accumulation, feed use and changes to surrounding coastal habitats when farms are not properly managed. Responsible management of water quality, feed, disease and farm effluent is therefore important for reducing these impacts. WWF also identifies its Aquaculture Improvement Project as an alternative for improving the sustainability of this seafood source.

description: A cold-water lobster with large claws, associated with the northwest Atlantic and prized for its sweet meat.
context: WWF highlights entanglement of endangered North Atlantic right whales and interactions with other protected species such as seabirds, sea turtles, sharks, rays and marine mammals in the North Atlantic trap-and-pot fishery. Discard rates and non-ETP bycatch are low and benthic impacts are moderate to low, but the documented whale impact is serious enough to support an Avoid rating.

description: A burrowing coastal clam associated with sandy and muddy intertidal areas and collected for fresh seafood.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kepah collected by hand as Best Choice. Kepah are filter-feeding clams that live buried in sandy or muddy coastal and estuarine sediments. Hand collection is a relatively selective harvesting method that produces little bycatch and generally requires no heavy fishing gear. However, maintaining appropriate harvest levels and protecting coastal habitats remain important for ensuring that natural clam populations can replenish.

description: A filter-feeding cockle that lives in muddy coastal flats and is widely harvested and farmed in Southeast Asia.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kerang farmed using bottom culture as Best Choice. Kerang are filter-feeding shellfish commonly cultured on intertidal mudflats and obtain their food naturally by filtering plankton and organic particles from the surrounding water. This means farming generally requires no external feed, reducing pressure on wild fish resources. Responsible site selection, stocking density and water-quality management remain important for maintaining healthy shellfish beds and surrounding coastal habitats.

description: A cold-water mussel that grows on rocky shores and other firm surfaces and is widely eaten around the world.
context: WWF rates Kupang from Norway collected by hand as Best Choice. Kupang are filter-feeding mussels that obtain their food naturally from plankton and suspended particles in the surrounding water. Hand collection is a relatively selective harvesting method that avoids the use of mobile fishing gear and generally causes limited disturbance to seabed habitats. Maintaining appropriate harvesting levels remains important for allowing natural mussel populations to replenish.

description: A tropical green-shelled mussel that grows in sheltered coastal waters and is commonly farmed on rafts.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Kupang / Siput Sudu farmed using raft culture as Best Choice. These mussels are filter feeders that obtain nutrients naturally from the surrounding water and therefore generally require no external feed during cultivation. Raft farming can produce seafood with relatively low pressure on wild fish stocks and limited direct seabed disturbance. Responsible site selection and farm management are still important to prevent excessive accumulation of organic material beneath farming areas.

description: A coastal clam found in shallow sandy and muddy areas and collected as a common shellfish food.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Lala collected by hand as Best Choice. Lala are filter-feeding clams commonly found buried in sandy or muddy coastal and estuarine habitats. Hand collection is relatively selective, produces little bycatch and avoids the use of mobile fishing gear that can cause greater seabed disturbance. Maintaining appropriate harvesting levels and protecting intertidal and estuarine habitats remain important for allowing natural populations to replenish.

description: A burrowing carpet clam associated with shallow coastal sediments and harvested in Malaysian waters.
context: WWF rates Siput Retak Seribu from Peninsular Malaysia caught using dredgers as Reduce. Siput Retak Seribu is a burrowing clam that lives within sandy and muddy coastal sediments. Dredging physically disturbs the seabed while collecting shellfish and can affect other bottom-dwelling organisms and habitats. Managing dredging intensity, harvesting pressure and the condition of shellfish beds is therefore important for maintaining the sustainability of this fishery.

description: Oysters are filter-feeding bivalves commonly grown on racks or rafts in sheltered coastal waters.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Tiram farmed using rack-and-raft culture as Best Choice. Tiram are filter-feeding shellfish that obtain their food naturally from plankton and suspended particles, meaning oyster farming generally requires no external feed. Rack-and-raft systems can produce seafood with relatively low pressure on wild fish resources and limited use of destructive fishing gear. Appropriate farm siting, stocking density and water-quality management remain important for reducing local environmental impacts.

description: A spiny lobster associated with tropical coastal and reef habitats, recognised by its long antennae and hard shell.
context: WWF rates Udang Karang from Peninsular Malaysia caught using trawl as Avoid. Udang Karang is a bottom-dwelling lobster associated with coastal waters and seabed habitats. Trawl fishing can capture non-target fish and other marine organisms while disturbing seabed communities where the gear contacts the bottom. Lobsters can also be vulnerable to excessive harvesting when mature breeding individuals are heavily removed, adding to the sustainability concerns associated with this source.

description: A large Western Australian rock lobster with a robust shell and long antennae, prized for its sweet meat.
context: WWF rates Western Australian Rock Lobster Best Choice. The guide says the pot/trap fishery is unlikely to cause significant damage to endangered, threatened and protected species, has low discard rates with discarded catch released alive, and has negligible overall ecosystem impact. Stock status is described as healthy. Traps can affect reef habitat, but WWF considers that impact generally low compared with other fishing methods.

description: A flattened lobster with broad antennae and a hard, rough body, generally associated with warm coastal waters.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Udang Lobok caught using trawl as Avoid. Udang Lobok are bottom-dwelling crustaceans that live on sandy and muddy seabeds. Trawling operates directly across these habitats and can capture non-target fish and other marine organisms while disturbing seabed communities. The combination of bycatch, habitat disturbance and fishing pressure creates significant sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A squid with a compact body and fins, living in tropical marine waters and commonly caught by trawlers.
context: WWF rates Malaysian squid fisheries Avoid. The S.O.S. guide says Malaysian squid stock status is unknown because of data deficiency and identifies trawling as a common capture method. WWF describes trawls as highly detrimental because they are non-selective, prone to habitat destruction and can create bycatch of endangered, threatened and protected species. Those combined uncertainties and impacts support Avoid.

description: A common tropical squid with an elongated body and fins, widely used in Southeast Asian seafood dishes.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Sotong Biasa / Cumit-cumit caught using trawl as Avoid. This squid is a fast-growing cephalopod commonly found in coastal and shelf waters. Although squid generally have short life cycles and can reproduce relatively quickly, trawl fishing can capture non-target marine species and disturb seabed habitats where the gear contacts the bottom. These fishing-method impacts create additional sustainability concerns for this source.

description: A cuttlefish with a broad body and internal cuttlebone, found in shallow tropical marine waters.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Sotong Katak caught using trawl as Avoid. Sotong Katak is a bottom-associated cuttlefish commonly found in shallow coastal waters over sandy and muddy habitats. Trawl fishing operates across these seabed environments and can capture non-target marine organisms while disturbing benthic habitats. Although cuttlefish generally have relatively short life cycles, fishing pressure and the environmental impacts associated with trawling remain important sustainability concerns.

description: A larger tropical squid with broad fins along the mantle, commonly found in coastal waters and valued as seafood.
context: WWF rates Malaysian Sotong Mengabang caught using traps as Reduce. Sotong Mengabang is a fast-growing cephalopod commonly found in shallow coastal waters around coral reefs, seagrass beds and other structured habitats. Squid generally have short life cycles and can reproduce relatively quickly, but their populations can still be affected by high fishing pressure and changing environmental conditions. Trap fishing is relatively selective and generally has limited seabed impact, but appropriate management of fishing effort remains important for maintaining sustainable populations.
